
# Profile mixture model results

```{r}
# Values for the text (2026-10-22), from the model samples defined in
# PMM_102_calibration_model.R and PMM_103_informant_model.R.
n_cog_model <- nrow(inhcap_cog)
n_inf_model <- nrow(inhcap_jorm)

weighted_shares <- function(d) {
  w <- tapply(d$HCAP16WGTR, as.integer(haven::zap_labels(d$vs1hcapdxeap)), sum)
  100 * w / sum(w)
}
fmt_shares <- function(p) sprintf("%.1f%%, %.1f%%, and %.1f%%", p[1], p[2], p[3])
prior_cog <- weighted_shares(inhcap_cog)
prior_inf <- weighted_shares(inhcap_jorm)
```

The profile mixture model (PMM) gives each HRS/HCAP participant a probability of membership in each of the 3 classes of the HRS/HCAP Algorithm (Normal, MCI, and Dementia; Manly et al., 2022). Two models are needed because the core interview follows 2 routes: participants who complete cognitive testing provide test scores and a self-rating of memory, and participants who do not complete testing may have an informant report (the Jorm IQCODE; Jorm, 1994) and no test scores. The *cognition model* applies to the `r format(n_cog_model, big.mark = ",")` participants with at least 1 cognitive test score or a self-rating of memory (@fig-pmm-model). Its indicators are the 8 cognitive tests of the core interview (orientation to date; animal naming; object naming; naming the President and Vice President; delayed word recall; number series; serial 7 subtraction; and backward counting from 20) and self-rated memory (`PD102`). The *informant model* applies to the `r n_inf_model` participants with no test score or self-rating who have an informant report, and its only indicator is the IQCODE. Each participant receives probabilities from 1 model.

The PMM uses the same information as the core algorithm (Appendix 1 of the manuscript), so that differences in agreement with the HRS/HCAP Algorithm reflect the classification method and not access to different data. We did not include the core interview items on limitations in activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL). These items do not say why a limitation is present, and a limitation with a physical cause would raise the probability of dementia; a participant with hip arthritis who reports difficulty dressing is one example. We also did not include immediate word recall, which adds little information beyond delayed recall (Jones et al., 2024) and is not part of the core algorithm.

Each model is fit in 2 steps. In the first step (calibration), a known-class mixture model is estimated in HRS/HCAP with class membership fixed at the HRS/HCAP Algorithm classification (`vs1hcapdxeap`); participants with known class membership are what Muthén (2002) calls training data. Estimation is by maximum likelihood with robust standard errors (MLR), using the HCAP sampling weight (`HCAP16WGTR`), strata, and clusters (the Mplus SUBPOPULATION option is not available with KNOWNCLASS). In the second step (scoring), every parameter is fixed at its calibration value, the known class is removed, and Mplus computes each participant's posterior probability of each class by Bayes' rule. The class proportions, which are the priors in Bayes' rule, are also fixed: at the survey-weighted shares of the HRS/HCAP Algorithm classes in each model's sample (cognition model `r fmt_shares(prior_cog)` for Normal, MCI, and Dementia; informant model `r fmt_shares(prior_inf)`). We compute them outside Mplus, because Mplus estimates known-class proportions from unweighted counts even when a weight is specified. This report scores the same HRS/HCAP participants used for calibration, so the agreement with the HRS/HCAP Algorithm reported here is in-sample and is likely optimistic. Analysis A3_2 applies the fixed scoring models to HRS core respondents age 65 and older interviewed from 2016 to 2022.

### Class assignments

The scoring step gives each participant 3 probabilities that sum to 1. Their survey-weighted averages estimate the marginal class rates implied by the model. Assigning each participant to the most likely class gives a separate set of rates, which need not reproduce those averages. Both are shown alongside the Manly-Jones algorithm rates below.

For probability-allocation agreement, each cross-table cell is the sum of the survey weight times the predicted class probability among participants in the comparator category. A participant with probabilities of 0.90, 0.01, and 0.09 contributes those fractions of their weight to Normal, MCI, and Dementia. No replicated records or integer allocations are used. Kappas for the most likely class are reported separately. All statistics are computed before rounding for display.
